title: Spend structure before spending waste
subtitle: The lane-packing algorithms that let a GPU broker pad 0.4 percent and keep two different cards at a 99.9 percent cache hit rate

stats.label: lane reuses, against 0.49 new lanes per second
key-value cache hit rate on both cards

lede: Padding is the tax a GPU pays for batching sequences of different lengths, and cache misses are the tax it pays for mixing prompts that share nothing. A queue that moves bytes knows about neither. I built the broker in my inference pipeline to know about both, with a set of algorithms that decide, for every item, which batch it belongs in and when it goes. Two prompts can share a batch cheaply only if they share cacheable structure, the system prompt, the few-shot block, the tool schema, and have similar lengths. Length is cheap to read. Shared structure is not, and the broker must never parse prompts or know the model.
quote: A poisoned cache is worse than a restart.
evidence: Token-aware scheduling: shape signatures from ordered prefix hashes and 2,048 rolling lanes per shape, keeping two cards at a 99.9% key-value cache hit rate.
Batch padding optimisation: a waste threshold that rises from one percent to ten percent with lane pressure, with a 16-token floor and a 128-token cap, for 0.421% padding.
Message broker and queue design: lane reuse at 17,800/s against 0.49 new lanes per second, and 12.3 B tokens received and routed with a difference of zero.
Distributed systems correctness: a dispatch loop that yields after 100 milliseconds, after a fill of 3,099 batches blocked heartbeats long enough for healthy GPUs to be declared dead.
author: Corey James
